q: Binary search on a sorted array of n items takes how many steps in the worst case?
why: Each step halves the search range, so it ends after about log₂ n steps.

q: Which data structure drives a breadth-first search (BFS)?
why: BFS visits nodes level by level: first in, first out — a queue. DFS is the one that uses a stack.

q: What is the worst-case running time of quicksort?
why: If the pivot is always the smallest or largest item (e.g. sorted input with a naive pivot), every split is n−1 / 0, giving O(n²). Random pivots make this very unlikely.

q: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys in sorted order?
why: In-order visits left subtree, node, right subtree — exactly ascending order in a BST.

q: Detecting a cycle in a linked list with O(1) extra space uses…
options: A hash set of visited nodes
why: A slow pointer moves 1 step and a fast one 2 steps; if there is a cycle they must meet. No extra memory needed.

q: Dijkstra's algorithm can give wrong answers when the graph has…
why: Dijkstra assumes a settled node's distance never improves, which negative edges can break. Bellman–Ford handles them.

q: In a binary min-heap of n items, removing the minimum costs…
why: Reading the minimum is O(1), but removing it moves the last item to the root and sifts it down the tree's height: O(log n).

q: Average-case time to look up a key in a hash map is…
why: A good hash spreads keys across buckets, so a lookup checks only a few entries on average. Many collisions can push it towards O(n).

q: In Go, what happens when you write to a nil map (var m map[string]int; m["a"] = 1)?
why: Reading a nil map returns zero values, but writing panics: 'assignment to entry in nil map'. Create it first with make(map[string]int).

q: A Go function runs defer print(1); defer print(2); defer print(3). What is printed?
why: Deferred calls run last-in, first-out when the function returns: 3, then 2, then 1.

q: What happens when you send a value on a closed channel in Go?
why: Sending on a closed channel panics. Receiving from one is fine: you get the zero value and ok == false.

q: In Go, len("हिंदी") returns…
why: len counts bytes, not letters. हिंदी is 5 Unicode code points × 3 bytes each in UTF-8 = 15. utf8.RuneCountInString gives 5.

q: A send on an unbuffered Go channel completes when…
options: The value is copied to the buffer
why: An unbuffered channel has no storage: sender and receiver must meet, so the send blocks until someone receives.

q: For two Java Strings a and b, what does a == b compare?
why: == on objects checks identity. Use a.equals(b) to compare the text.

q: How many null keys can a java.util.HashMap hold?
why: HashMap allows exactly one null key (and any number of null values). Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap allow none.

q: An int field in a Java class that is never assigned holds…
why: Fields get default values (0, false, null). Local variables are different: using one unassigned is a compile error.

q: What does typeof null return in JavaScript?
why: A bug from JavaScript's first version that can never be fixed without breaking the web: typeof null is "object".

q: In JavaScript, 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is…
why: 0.1 and 0.2 can't be stored exactly in binary floating point; the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a small tolerance instead.

q: What does ['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt) return?
why: map passes (value, index): parseInt('1', 0) = 1, parseInt('2', 1) = NaN (radix 1 is invalid), parseInt('3', 2) = NaN ('3' isn't binary).

q: setTimeout(fn, 0) and Promise.resolve().then(fn2) are scheduled together. Which runs first?
why: Promise callbacks are microtasks and run as soon as the current script finishes, before the next task such as a timer.

q: Which HTTP status code means a new resource was created?
why: 201 Created, usually with a Location header pointing to the new resource.

q: Which HTTP method is defined as idempotent (repeating it has the same effect as once)?
why: PUT replaces the resource with the same body each time. POST may create a new item on every call, and PATCH isn't guaranteed idempotent.

q: Adding an index to a database column mainly…
options: Speeds up reads that filter on it, slows writes a little
why: An index is an extra sorted structure: lookups get much faster, but every insert or update must keep it in sync.

q: In ACID, what does the I stand for?
why: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work.

q: By the CAP theorem, during a network partition a distributed system must choose between…
why: When nodes can't talk, you either refuse some requests (stay consistent) or answer with possibly stale data (stay available).

q: A cache that writes every update to the cache and the database at the same time is called…
why: Write-through keeps cache and DB in sync on every write. Write-back writes to the cache first and flushes to the DB later.

q: Amazon S3 is what kind of storage?
why: S3 stores objects (data + metadata) by key in buckets. EBS is block storage, EFS is a network file system.

q: Which command replays your commits on top of another branch, rewriting their history?
why: Rebase creates new commits on the new base, giving a straight history. Don't rebase commits others have already pulled.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the four conditions for a deadlock?
why: The condition is NO preemption: resources can't be taken away. Allowing preemption is one way to prevent deadlock.

q: In Flutter, calling setState() inside a State object…
why: setState marks this State dirty, so its build method runs again on the next frame, along with the subtree it returns.
